intro_en:
The Israel National Trail descends into the Timna Valley and is exposed to the landscapes, colours and geology of the Eilat Mountains. At the heart of the route: wonderful lookouts over the Timna Crater and the colourful, unique Sasgon Valley.

 Shaharut - Be'er Milhan (51)
 Timna - Be'er Ora (53)
character_en: (Walking from north to south) We begin with a gentle descent and continue to a fairly steep descent (about 450 metres of vertical drop) on a relatively comfortable road. We end the walk with a flat section in the Timna Valley
transport_en: At the end point: a bus stop on the Arava road, 3 km from the visitor centre. During the park's opening hours, there is a good chance of hitching a ride to the park entrance
pois_en: Lookouts from the top of the Timna cliffs. Sasgon Valley, the Sasgon dune
important_en: The Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA) places a water trailer at the overnight campsites in the area. Confirm this with the regional ranger when planning the route.
At Be'er Ora it is possible to stock up on food at the minimarket, and to its west there is a campsite for trail hikers.
description_en:
We leave the overnight campsite at Be'er Milhan along a dirt road heading east. The well, which held brackish water, was built during the British Mandate period and was used to water the Bedouin herds until the 1980s. Today it is no longer in use.
After walking a few hundred metres, we meet the Israel National Trail marking. The trail and the road climb gently up Nahal Matok, a tributary of Nahal Milhan. Maps mark another well in this area, Be'er Matok, but we will not find it on the ground; the well was neglected and became blocked over the years.
At a junction where a green-marked trail branches off to the right towards the south-west, we continue with the Israel National Trail and a blue-marked road towards the south-east, to the watershed between the Uvda Valley and the Timna Valley.
A little before crossing the watershed line, we pass a trail junction where the blue road we have been walking meets a red-marked trail. This trail circles the entire Timna Crater.
The right-hand branch of the red trail turns west and south towards Har Berekh and Ma'ale Gadna. The Israel National Trail continues with the left-hand branch of the red trail eastwards, to Ma'ale Milhan and the Sasgon Valley.
Those who need to exit towards Road 12, or who wish to arrange a pick-up with a private vehicle coming from that road, can leave after Ma'ale Milhan to the left with the red marking, and walk a beautiful trail of about 5 km to Har Berekh, which is reached by a road suitable, at slow speed, for any vehicle.
After crossing a low spur, we reach the start of the descent to the Arava. On a terrace below the trail, a stream that drains into the Timna Valley cuts its way down, and we can follow the course of the channel between the tops of the Timna cliffs, the rock walls that enclose the Timna Valley from the west. Far off, beyond the cliffs, a dark mountain can be seen: Har Timna (Mount Timna).
We descend to the Sasgon Valley in the Timna Valley (around the marking of Nahal Mangan on the maps), from an elevation of about 600 metres down to 150 metres. In the section of the descent down to the top of Ma'ale Milhan, the trail is gentle and comfortable, and after it the descent is fairly steep.
We pass above the Timna cliffs with beautiful lookout points over the Timna Crater. From the lookouts one can see that the shape of the Timna Crater resembles that of the other Negev craters (makhteshim): an enclosed valley surrounded by high cliffs.
In the process of the Timna Crater's formation, an ancient block of hard basement rock, originating in the primordial rocks that formed the Earth, was uplifted and exposed at the surface. The ancient rock block rose into younger, softer rock layers of sandstone and marine sedimentary rocks, which were later removed by erosion. Thus the dark mass of Har Timna remained at the heart of the crater that formed around it.
Later in the geological history, when the Arava Rift was formed, the eastern flank of the crater was removed. The result of these processes as it appears today: a horseshoe-shaped crater with Har Timna rising at the centre of its base.
Two streams drain the crater: north of the mountain, Nahal Timna flows to the Arava, and south of the mountain Nahal Nehushtan drains the valley. In the crater walls a geological section is exposed, of rocks formed over long periods. At the bottom of the section, close to the crater floor, are ancient sandstones. We will see them in the Timna Valley at Solomon's Pillars, the 'Mushroom' and the 'Arches'. The later layers at the top of the geological section, those seen at the top of the cliffs around the valley, are of limestone and dolomite, marine sedimentary rocks. The fossils seen beside the trail attest that these rocks were formed in a marine environment.
After a while, the view of the Arava and of the dark hills of the Sasgon Valley opens up ahead of us in the direction of walking. We complete the descent into the Timna Valley with the steep part of Ma'ale Milhan.
From the bottom of the ascent we continue alongside the sandy tributaries of Nahal Mangan to the Sasgon Valley. On the way we can see how the valley earned its name (Sasgon, 'multicoloured'): hills, rocks and cliffs in a variety of colours, black, grey, yellowish, pink and shades of red.
On the southern slope of one of the hills in the Sasgon Valley is a delightful dune. From 2007 to 2019 a campaign was waged, led by the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI) together with Arava residents and other environmental organisations, against plans to build a hotel zone in the Sasgon Valley. The campaign succeeded and the construction plans were cancelled.
The Israel National Trail continues between Har Mikhrot and the Sasgon hills, crossing the wide channel of Nahal Timna on its way south to the Timna Park visitor centre.
nearby_en: Timna Park: with a wealth of sites and short and medium-length trails through wonderful sandstone landscapes and alongside copper mining shafts. Entry to Timna Park is subject to a fee; walking the Israel National Trail through the park is free of charge for trail hikers.
Har Timna (included in segment 53 of the Israel National Trail).
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
